newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RAAF gives AlliedSignal hope on Hawk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RAAF gives AlliedSignal hope on Hawk.

text.p: The Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) is offering AlliedSignal Inc new hope of selling its F124 engine on the popular British Aerospace Hawk trainer-attack aircraft, displacing Rolls-Royce Plc.
"We've asked British Aerospace to have a competition between the two engines," said Group Captain Graeme Cooper, head of the RAAF's programme to buy up to 40 Hawks.
"It will be decided sometime in early 1997," he told Reuters.

There are two main variants of the Hawk. British Aerospace designed the original model and builds it for export while McDonnell Douglas Corp builds a U.S. Navy version, the T-45 Goshawk, which it is trying to export.
The Rolls-Royce Adour powers both versions but AlliedSignal has been working with McDonnell Douglas to offer the new F124 engine on the U.S. version.
Australia was a possible launch order for the F124-powered Goshawk but it rejected the McDonnell aircraft in September, two months before announcing its choice of the British Aerospace Hawk.
"The reason that we wanted to look at the F124 engines is that it is far newer, it is fully modular, and it has several other benefits," Cooper said noting the U.S. engine's lightness.
The competition would be assessed on the basis of price and performance, he said.

An Australian defence official familiar with the programme said the F124's presumed advantage in fuel consumption was not necessarily important to Australia, which needed the aircraft for only short missions. But maintainability and reliability were significant factors, aside from the obvious issue of cost.
More than 700 Hawks, of both variants, have been sold since British Aerospace began building it for Britain's Royal Air Force in the 1970s.
